summary: Clarifies issues about subnetting IP networks by providing a standard subnet table. It is informational and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A cheat sheet listing the sizes into which you can slice an address block.

subtitle: A reference table of every IPv4 subnet mask from /1 to /32, with the host and network counts each one gives.

tldr.problem: Subnetting rules were sometimes misread, and networks had grown larger and more complex than the earlier subnetting guidelines anticipated.
tldr.mechanism: The memo lists every variable length subnet mask from 1 to 32 bits in hex, CIDR and dotted decimal form, with address counts and classful equivalents, then works through Class B and Class C subnetting examples.
tldr.outcome: It is informational only and its status is Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1860 and no newer RFC is listed as replacing it.

today: RFC 1878 is Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1860, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. The memo itself was only informational and never specified a standard.

sections.title: Why a Subnet Table
sections.content:
RFC 1878 is an informational memo, so it does not define an Internet standard. It says that network growth since STD 5 (RFC 950) and STD 3 (RFC 1123) had made subnetting larger and more complex, and that those RFCs had sometimes been misinterpreted, which caused confusion about proper subnetting.

The memo is meant as a companion to the subnetting RFC and the Host Requirements RFC. It itemizes the possible IPv4 subnet values and adds hex and decimal forms, classful equivalents and the number of addresses in each block, with the emphasis on Class C subnets.
sections.plainLanguage: People kept getting confused about how to cut up address blocks, so the authors wrote one clear chart that everyone can check.

sections.title: The Variable Length Subnet Table
sections.content:
The main table runs from a 1-bit mask to a 32-bit mask. Each row gives the mask in hex (for example FF.FF.FF.00), the CIDR prefix form (/24), the dotted decimal mask (255.255.255.0), the number of addresses, and the traditional class equivalent.

The address counts halve with every extra bit. A /8 holds 16 M addresses and is one Class A, a /16 holds 64 K and is one Class B, and a /24 holds 256 and is one Class C. Below that, a /25 is half of a Class C, a /30 holds 4 addresses, and a /32 is described as a single host route.
sections.plainLanguage: Every time you add one more bit to the mask, each block gets cut in half. A /32 is so small that it is just one single computer.

sections.title: Subnetting Class B and Class C Networks
sections.content:
The memo then shows what the subnetting bits do. Table 1-1 covers a Class B network and Table 1-2 covers a Class C network, which the memo says is identical to extended Class B subnets. For each mask it lists the number of nets, the hosts per subnet, the network addresses, the host address range and the broadcast address.

For example, a Class B network with a 2-bit subnet (mask 255.255.192.0) gives 4 nets of 16382 hosts each. A Class C network with a 2-bit subnet (mask 255.255.255.192) gives 4 nets of 62 hosts each, with broadcast addresses at N.N.N.63, N.N.N.127, N.N.N.191 and N.N.N.255.
sections.plainLanguage: The chart shows what happens when you cut one big block into equal pieces: how many pieces you get, and how many computers fit in each piece.

sections.title: All-Zeros and All-Ones Subnets
sections.content:
Tables 1-1 and 1-2 include the all-zeros and all-ones subnets, following what the memo calls the current, standards-based practice of using all definable subnets, citing RFC 1812.

For completeness, Tables 2-1 and 2-2 show the older calculation that excludes the all-zeros and all-ones subnets. Many vendors only supported subnetting on that premise, but the memo states plainly that this practice is obsolete and that modern software will be able to use all definable networks. For example, from a /24 block with 2 subnet bits, the older rule yields 2 effective subnets of 62 hosts, where the newer counting yields 4 subnets.
sections.plainLanguage: Old rules said you had to throw away the first and last slice. The memo says that rule is out of date, so you can use every slice.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo contains a one-line Security Considerations section: security issues are not discussed. It is a lookup table and defines no protocol behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: It is just a chart of numbers, so there is nothing to protect here.
